before: For numbers in R, + adds, - subtracts, and * multiplies.
after:
For numbers in R, + adds, - subtracts, and * multiplies.

Subtraction takes two numeric operands and returns their difference; multiplication returns their product. Neither expression reassigns its operands.
```r
cat(7 - 2, "\n", sep = "")
cat(3 * 4, "\n", sep = "")
```
It prints:
```text
5
12
```

before: & and | operate elementwise. && and || are short-circuit operators for scalar conditions; supplying a vector longer than one is an error in this tested runtime.
after:
& and | operate elementwise. && and || are short-circuit operators for scalar conditions; supplying a vector longer than one is an error in this tested runtime.

The elementwise | combines corresponding logical entries. && and || use scalar logical choices: false on the left decides &&, and true on the left decides || without evaluating the right expression.
```r
cat(c(TRUE, FALSE) | c(FALSE, FALSE), sep = ",")
cat("\n")
cat(FALSE && TRUE, "\n", sep = "")
cat(TRUE || FALSE, "\n", sep = "")
```
It prints:
```text
TRUE,FALSE
FALSE
TRUE
```

before: is.na(values) marks missing entries. ! negates those flags. Combining !is.na(values) & (values > 2) rejects missing entries while retaining known qualifying values. Both masks are evaluated elementwise: & is not short-circuiting, and FALSE & NA is FALSE.
after:
is.na(values) returns one logical missingness flag per entry. ! negates those flags. Combining !is.na(values) & (values > 2) rejects missing entries while retaining known qualifying values. Both masks are evaluated elementwise: & is not short-circuiting, and FALSE & NA is FALSE.


```r
values <- c(1, NA, 4)
cat(values[!is.na(values) & (values > 2)], "\n", sep = "")
```
It prints:
```text
4
```

after:
is.finite(values) takes a numeric vector and returns one logical flag per value: TRUE for finite values and FALSE for NA, NaN and infinities.


```r
values <- c(2, NA, NaN, Inf, -Inf)
cat(is.finite(values), sep = ",")
```
It prints:
```text
TRUE,FALSE,FALSE,FALSE,FALSE
```

[[ with index 1 and $ with fixed name score both extract the stored component itself here, not a one-component list. Each returns the numeric value 7.

after:
as.character first obtains the labels. as.numeric can then parse valid numeric text; unsuitable text can produce NA with a warning, so real input still needs validation.

after:
numeric(length(values)) can allocate a result vector before a loop. Avoid repeatedly growing large vectors without measuring the cost.

For a nonnegative whole-number n, numeric(n) creates a double vector of length n initialized to zero. In particular numeric(0) creates no entries, which is why the quiz's seq_along loop has no iterations.
```r
cat(length(numeric(0)), "\n", sep = "")
cat(numeric(2), sep = ",")
```
It prints:
```text
0

```

before: The last evaluated expression supplies the result unless return exits earlier. Returning a value is distinct from printing it.
after:
The last evaluated expression supplies the result unless return exits earlier. Returning a value is distinct from printing it.

return(value) leaves the current function immediately with that value. This function accepts one number; a negative input returns zero early, while another input reaches the final expression.
```r
nonnegative <- function(x) {
  if (x < 0) return(0)
  x
}
cat(nonnegative(-2), nonnegative(3), sep = ",")
```
It prints:
```text
0,3
```

before: force(x) evaluates the promise for x now. It is useful before returning a closure that should retain the current argument value. It does not recursively force every promise stored elsewhere.
after:
force(x) evaluates the promise for x now. It is useful before returning a closure that should retain the current argument value. It does not recursively force every promise stored elsewhere.

Here force receives the promised x argument and evaluates it even though use is FALSE. The supplied stop call receives a diagnostic message and raises that error, so no value 7 is returned. This deliberately failing example contrasts with the successful lazy call below.
```r
choose_now <- function(x, use) {
  force(x)
  if (use) x else 7
}
choose_now(stop("evaluated"), FALSE)
```
This stops with evaluated.

before: typeof reports the underlying R type. class reports the class used by many higher-level operations; setting a class label does not validate that the object satisfies its intended contract. Special attributes can alter interpretation without replacing the stored numbers.
after:
typeof reports the underlying R type. class reports the class used by many higher-level operations; setting a class label does not validate that the object satisfies its intended contract. Special attributes can alter interpretation without replacing the stored numbers.

class takes an object and reports its higher-level class label. For this ordinary double vector the label is numeric, while typeof reports the storage type double.
```r
values <- c(10, 20)
cat(class(values), "\n", sep = "")
cat(typeof(values), "\n", sep = "")
```
It prints:
```text
numeric
double
```

before: lapply returns one list element per input element, preserving a list result even when values are simple. vapply additionally requires each function result to match an explicit length and compatible type template.
after:
lapply returns one list element per input element, preserving a list result even when values are simple. vapply additionally requires each function result to match an explicit length and compatible type template.

lapply receives a list and a function to call on each element. It returns a list of the function results; these two sums remain separate list elements rather than becoming the atomic vector returned by the vapply example.
```r
values <- list(c(1, 2), c(4, 5))
result <- lapply(values, sum)
cat(typeof(result), "\n", sep = "")
cat(result[[1]], result[[2]], sep = ",")
```
It prints:

```text
3,9
```

before: gsub replaces every match and returns strings; sub replaces only the first match in each string. Neither evaluates the replacement as R code. Complex regular expressions and unbounded external input need separate performance and validation limits.
after:
gsub replaces every match and returns strings; sub replaces only the first match in each string. Neither evaluates the replacement as R code. Complex regular expressions and unbounded external input need separate performance and validation limits.

sub receives a pattern, replacement and text. With fixed = TRUE the dot is literal; sub returns only the first replacement in each string, while gsub replaces both matches here. Neither changes text.
```r
text <- "a.b.c"
cat(sub(".", "-", text, fixed = TRUE), "\n", sep = "")
cat(gsub(".", "-", text, fixed = TRUE), "\n", sep = "")
```
It prints:
```text
a-b.c
a-b-c
```

before: library attaches an installed package’s exported names to the search path. Another binding can mask an unqualified name. package::name selects that package’s exported object directly without attaching all of its names; it does not install a missing package.
after:
library attaches an installed package’s exported names to the search path. Another binding can mask an unqualified name. package::name selects that package’s exported object directly without attaching all of its names; it does not install a missing package.

library(stats) attaches the already installed stats package so its exported median can be found by an unmasked name. This fresh-script example installs nothing; the separate masked-name example below still shows why explicit stats::median can matter.
```r
library(stats)
cat(median(c(1, 9, 5)), "\n", sep = "")
```
It prints:
```text
5
```

before: sprintf("%.1f", x) formats a number as text with one decimal place; it changes display, not the stored number. sd estimates sample standard deviation using denominator n - 1; its unit matches the observations. var is its square and has squared units. quantile estimates cut points; R supports several definitions, so type = 7 is explicit here.
after:
sprintf("%.1f", x) formats a number as text with one decimal place; it changes display, not the stored number. sd estimates sample standard deviation using denominator n - 1; its unit matches the observations. var(x) receives numeric observations and returns their sample variance, the square of sample standard deviation, in squared units. quantile receives observations and requested probabilities and returns estimated cut points; R supports several definitions, so type = 7 is explicit here.

Here probs = c(0.25, 0.75) requests the lower and upper quartiles.
```r
x <- c(1, 2, 3)
cat(sprintf("%.1f", var(x)), "\n", sep = "")
cat(sprintf("%.1f", quantile(x, probs = c(0.25, 0.75), type = 7)), sep = ",")
```
It prints:
```text
1.0
1.5,2.5
```

before: glm with family = binomial() uses the logit link by default for a binary response. A 0/1 vector records failures/successes. The linear predictor is log-odds, log(p / (1 - p)); it is not itself a probability.
after:
glm with family = binomial() uses the logit link by default for a binary response. A 0/1 vector records failures/successes. The linear predictor is log-odds, log(p / (1 - p)); it is not itself a probability.

binomial() takes no explicit argument here and returns a family-configuration object with the default logit link. glm uses that configuration to fit the binary-response model; binomial() does not itself fit a model or return predicted probabilities.

log(x) uses the natural logarithm when no base is supplied. With probability p = 0.25, log(p / (1 - p)) converts the odds to a negative log-odds value; it does not return a probability.
```r
p <- 0.25
cat(sprintf("%.3f", log(p / (1 - p))), "\n", sep = "")
```
It prints:
```text
-1.099
```

after:
Profiling identifies where time is spent, not which result is correct. Compare outputs and representative workloads before changing algorithms; warm-up and repeated measurements may matter. This bounded example writes a local profile file and verifies only the computed result plus a nonnegative elapsed measurement.

seq_len(n) receives a nonnegative whole-number length and returns integer positions 1 through n, or an empty integer vector when n is zero. In the shown measure(1000) call it supplies the bounded integers whose sum is timed.

after:
quote captures an R expression without evaluating it. eval evaluates that expression in a supplied environment; new.env(parent = baseenv()) gives this example a controlled lookup context for a known expression, not a security sandbox.

baseenv() takes no arguments and returns R's base environment, containing base operations such as +. Using it as the new environment's parent controls where missing names are looked up; it does not restrict what arbitrary evaluated code is allowed to do.

sessionInfo records the R version, platform and loaded package information. RNGkind describes random-generator configuration; options can also affect behavior and formatting. Saving metadata helps explain a run but does not by itself recreate dependencies, input data or operating-system behavior.


before: A bounded pipeline checks type, missingness and domain before summarizing. Here input is a finite numeric vector; is.finite excludes NA, NaN and infinities, and the accepted range is 1..60 minutes. head(valid, 3) caps the number of retained valid observations.
after:

after:

```ruby
puts copy.inspect
```

after:

before: Hash uses hash and eql? together to identify keys. Integer 1 and Float 1.0 compare equal with == but not with eql?, so they are distinct hash keys. A custom key type that overrides eql? must provide a consistent hash result for equal keys; do not mutate key identity fields while stored.
after:
Hash uses hash and eql? together to identify keys. Integer 1 and Float 1.0 compare equal with == but not with eql?, so they are distinct hash keys. A custom key type that overrides eql? must provide a consistent hash result for equal keys; do not mutate key identity fields while stored.

receiver.hash takes no explicit argument and returns an integer hash code. Objects that are eql? must produce equal hash codes; do not depend on a particular code remaining the same between processes. Here two equal arrays satisfy that rule.
```ruby
a = [1]
b = [1]
puts a.eql?(b)
puts a.hash == b.hash
```
It prints:
```text
true
true
```

before: Enumerable supplies iteration helpers to classes with each. map builds results from each block return; select keeps original elements with truthy block results; reject keeps those whose block results are false or nil.
after:
Enumerable supplies iteration helpers to classes with each. map builds results from each block return; select keeps original elements with truthy block results; reject keeps those whose block results are false or nil.

reject receives a block and returns a new array of the original elements for which that block is false or nil. The source array stays unchanged.
```ruby
values = [1, 2, 3, 4]
p values.reject { |n| n.even? }
p values
```
It prints:
```text
[1, 3]
[1, 2, 3, 4]
```

after:
Calling each without a block returns an Enumerator. lazy builds a demand-driven pipeline rather than eagerly computing a full intermediate collection; force materializes the requested lazy results.

The no-block each call takes no explicit argument here and returns an Enumerator rather than executing an iteration block. class reports the kind of the returned object.
```ruby

puts stream.class
```

```text
Enumerator
```

before: encode converts representation when possible; force_encoding only changes how existing bytes are interpreted. valid_encoding? checks whether bytes fit the label. Do not silently relabel corrupted external data as valid text.
after:
encode converts representation when possible; force_encoding only changes how existing bytes are interpreted. valid_encoding? checks whether bytes fit the label. Do not silently relabel corrupted external data as valid text.

encode receives a target encoding name and returns a converted String. In this ASCII example UTF-16LE needs two bytes for A; converting back recovers the text.
```ruby
text = "A"
converted = text.encode("UTF-16LE")
puts converted.bytesize
puts converted.encode("UTF-8")
```
It prints:
```text
2
A
```

force_encoding receives an encoding label and changes that same String's label without converting its bytes. dup first gives this example a separate mutable String. Relabeling its UTF-8 bytes for é as US-ASCII leaves two bytes that are invalid under the new label.
```ruby
text = "é".dup
text.force_encoding("US-ASCII")
puts text.bytesize
puts text.valid_encoding?
```
It prints:
```text
2
false
```

before: File.open(path, mode) with a block closes the file when the block exits, including through an exception. Mode w creates or truncates a file; read reads its contents. Use this only on the disposable fixture path.
after:
File.open(path, mode) with a block closes the file when the block exits, including through an exception. Mode w creates or truncates a file; read reads its contents. Use this only on the disposable fixture path.

Inside the block, file.write("read") receives the text to write to that open handle. It writes those bytes at the current position; the later File.read call shows the resulting contents. write returns the byte count, although this example does not use that return value.

after:
require "tempfile" loads the available library. Tempfile.create with a block creates a uniquely named temporary file and closes and removes it on block exit; do not construct predictable global temporary filenames yourself.

The array ["study", ".txt"] passed to Tempfile.create supplies a filename prefix and suffix. The block receives the open temporary file object; its generated name is not a stable value to assert.

before: File.basename extracts the final path component; File.join assembles components but does not prevent traversal or authorize a user-supplied path. rewind resets the file position to the beginning before read; otherwise reading immediately after writing would start at the end. end_with? tests a string suffix. The generated temporary path stays local here and is not printed.
after:
File.basename extracts the final path component; File.join assembles components but does not prevent traversal or authorize a user-supplied path. rewind resets the file position to the beginning before read; otherwise reading immediately after writing would start at the end. end_with? tests a string suffix. The generated temporary path stays local here and is not printed.

File.exist?(path) receives a path and returns true when that path exists, otherwise false. The final call below therefore checks removal after the temporary-file block, rather than merely checking whether the handle is closed.

require "csv" loads the available CSV library. CSV.parse handles delimiters inside quoted fields; splitting each line on commas does not. With headers: true, the first row names columns instead of becoming a data record.

With headers: true, CSV.parse returns a CSV::Table containing header-addressable CSV::Row objects. table.first selects the first data row; ["topic"] reads that row's field by header name. The returned field is still text.

after:
Time.utc constructs a known UTC instant. getlocal(offset) returns a new Time representation with that offset; it does not change the original. strftime formats fields using directives such as %Y year, %m month, %d day and %H:%M time.

The shown Time.utc arguments are year, month, day, hour and minute, in that order: (2025, 1, 1, 0, 30) means 00:30 on January 1, 2025 in UTC. Seconds are omitted and default to zero here.

after:
ARGV is the array of command-line argument strings. require "optparse" loads OptionParser; on("--minutes N", Integer) declares a value-bearing option and requests integer conversion. parse! consumes recognized options, leaving positional arguments in ARGV.

OptionParser.new returns the parser and supplies that parser to its construction block as options. Calls to options.on register rules on the same parser before parser.parse!(ARGV) processes the actual argument array.

before: A failed worker exception is re-raised to code joining or reading its value, so handle it deliberately. Thread.current.report_on_exception = false disables the automatic background diagnostic for this owned worker, not the exception itself; join still re-raises it. The worked case has no worker failure and prints only after joining. Interpreter scheduling and the GVL do not promise faster CPU execution or replace synchronization.
after:
A failed worker exception is re-raised to code joining or reading its value, so handle it deliberately. Thread.current.report_on_exception = false disables the automatic background diagnostic for this owned worker, not the exception itself; join still re-raises it. The worked case has no worker failure and prints only after joining. Interpreter scheduling and the GVL do not promise faster CPU execution or replace synchronization.

Thread.current takes no explicit arguments and returns the Thread object executing this call. Inside the worker block, the diagnostic-setting assignment therefore affects that worker, not a different thread.

before: A value conversion such as toLong or toDouble requests a different numeric representation. Kotlin does not generally assign a numeric variable to another numeric type implicitly.
after: A numeric conversion requests another representation; this lesson demonstrates Double.toInt. Kotlin does not generally assign a numeric variable to another numeric type implicitly. Other conversion names, such as toLong and toDouble, are optional API references, not additional operations required here.

before: Operations such as uppercase return another String. They do not rewrite a previous String value in place.
after: String values are immutable: building a different String does not rewrite the previous value. Case-conversion APIs such as uppercase are optional references beyond this interpolation example.

before: step chooses a positive stride; downTo creates descending progressions. A progression is not a promise of arbitrary floating-point steps.
after: This lesson compares closed and half-open integer bounds. Stride selection with step and descending progressions with downTo are optional API references, not required by this example. A progression is not a promise of arbitrary floating-point steps.

before: also exposes the value as it but returns the original context object. This differs from let even when their bodies look alike.

A data class generates useful operations such as equals, hashCode and copy from properties declared in its primary constructor. Properties declared only in the body are excluded from those generated comparisons and copies. copy(topics = newList) replaces that constructor property in the new instance. toMutableList() copies a list container, but its element references are still shared.
after:
A data class generates useful operations such as equals, hashCode and copy from properties declared in its primary constructor. Properties declared only in the body are excluded from those generated comparisons and copies. copy(topics = newList) replaces that constructor property in the new instance. toMutableList() copies a list container, but its element references are still shared.

Calling toMutableList on a list returns a new mutable outer list containing the same element references. Here adding to the copied container leaves the original container at one element; this is not a recursive clone.
```kotlin
fun main() {
    val original = mutableListOf("read")
    val copied = original.toMutableList()
    copied.add("write")
    println("${original.size} ${copied.size}")
}
```
Expected output: 1 2.

before: When multiple extensions have the same name, selection uses the receiver’s compile-time type. A derived object held in a Base variable therefore uses the Base extension. Actual overridable members still dispatch dynamically; a matching member also takes priority over an extension.
after:
When multiple extensions have the same name, selection uses the receiver’s compile-time type. A derived object held in a Base variable therefore uses the Base extension. Actual overridable members still dispatch dynamically; a matching member also takes priority over an extension.

The no-argument label call below has two different declared receiver types. The Base receiver returns "base" even though it holds a Detail object; the Detail receiver returns "detail". Neither extension overrides the other.
```kotlin
open class Base
class Detail : Base()
fun Base.label(): String = "base"
fun Detail.label(): String = "detail"
fun main() {
    val broad: Base = Detail()
    val narrow: Detail = Detail()
    println(broad.label())
    println(narrow.label())
}
```

is_dir(path) returns whether the supplied path names a directory. mkdir(path, 0700) attempts directory creation and returns success/failure; permissions are affected by the process umask and platform, so this is not a portable sandbox guarantee. ini_set(name, value) changes a configurable directive for this process and returns its previous value or false on failure. session_save_path(directory) selects file-session storage before starting the session and returns the previous path (or false on failure); setting it alone does not create the directory.

session_id() without an argument reads the current identifier; session_id($id) selects that identifier before the next session_start. session_destroy() destroys the stored data for the active session and returns success/failure, but does not automatically erase the in-memory $_SESSION array or delete a browser cookie. Those are separate responsibilities in a real web application.
